source.title: People v Salas (2025 NY Slip Op 03603)

captionLines: The People of the State of New York, Respondent,
dateLines: Appeal, by permission of the Chief Judge of the Court of Appeals, from an order of the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court in the First Judicial Department, entered October 19, 2023. The Appellate Division (1) modified, as a matter of discretion in the interest of justice, a judgment of the Supreme Court, Bronx County (John W. Carter, J.), which had convicted defendant, upon a jury verdict, of murder in the second degree; and (2) affirmed an order of that Supreme Court (Marsha D. Michael, J.), which had denied defendant's CPL 440.10 motion to vacate the judgment of conviction. The modification consisted of reducing the sentence of imprisonment to a term of 19 years to life. The Appellate Division affirmed the judgment as modified.

1. Where a transcript of on-the-record proceedings material to a defendant's claim under People v O'Rama (78 NY2d 270 [1991]) is missing, the proper remedy is a reconstruction hearing, provided that the defendant's conduct evidences a good-faith purpose to obtain prompt and effective reconstruction. Accordingly, in a criminal prosecution in which defendant first moved for a reconstruction hearing 9½ years after his conviction and nearly two years after a court reporter averred that the portion of the trial transcript relevant to the court's handling of a jury note was lost, defendant was not entitled to vacatur of his conviction based on the missing transcript. The trial court may have fully complied with O'Rama on the record; what transpired at relevant, on-the-record proceedings was not transcribed. The reconstruction remedy reflects a presumption of regularity that attaches to judicial proceedings and may be overcome only by substantial evidence. In light of the presumption of regularity, it cannot be assumed from a missing transcript alone that the court must have committed a mode of proceedings error during on-the-record proceedings. Such a presumption of irregularity would entitle defendants to vacatur of their convictions whenever a transcript of jury deliberation proceedings is lost, even where reconstruction could negate any prejudice and demonstrate that no error occurred. While there must be a reversal if a defendant shows they are entitled to a reconstruction hearing and that the missing transcript at issue cannot be reconstructed, defendant had not made that showing.

2. In a criminal prosecution, Supreme Court abused its discretion by denying defendant's CPL 440.10 motion claiming that defense counsel was ineffective without conducting an evidentiary hearing. A court "may deny" a CPL 440.10 motion summarily under enumerated circumstances, including where purported facts essential to the motion are unsupported by "sworn allegations" that "substantiat[e] or tend[ ] to substantiate" those facts (CPL 440.30 [4] [b]), or where such a fact "is contradicted by a court record or other official document" and "there is no reasonable possibility that [the] allegation is true" ( id. § 440.30 [4] [d]). Defendant's ineffective assistance claim could not be decided without first resolving questions of fact. Defense counsel's affirmation, together with the trial record, suggested that counsel may have lacked a strategic or otherwise legitimate basis for one or more of his actions relating to eyewitness identification testimony at the heart of the People's proof. Whether counsel in fact had such a basis for his conduct turned on factual information outside the record that should have been developed at an evidentiary hearing.

Darcel D. Clark, District Attorney , Bronx ( Gamaliel Marrero and Yael V. Levy of counsel), for respondent. I. Where defendant made only a perfunctory effort to facilitate reconstruction of missing stenographic minutes that may have revealed whether a jury note was submitted to the trial court and, if so, how the court addressed it, he has failed to overcome the presumption of regularity that attached to his trial or to establish that the court did not provide meaningful notice of the note. ( People v Parris , 4 NY3d 41 ; People v O'Rama , 78 NY2d 270; People v Parker , 32 NY3d 49 ; People v Harrison , 85 NY2d 794; People v Glass , 43 NY2d 283.) II. The Appellate Division providently affirmed the trial court's denial of defendant's CPL 440.10 motion without a hearing because the record supports the determination that counsel provided effective assistance. ( People v Delorbe , 35 NY3d 112 ; People v Satterfield , 66 NY2d 796; People v Jones , 24 NY3d 623 ; People v Cook , 34 NY3d 412 ; People v Branch , 83 NY2d 663.)

appearanceLikeLines.text: Milbank LLP , New York City ( Benjamin S. Brindis , Jed M. Schwartz , Emily Scarisbrick Weisberg and Alexa Savino of counsel), and Caprice R. Jenerson , Office of the Appellate Defender , New York City ( Margaret E. Knight of counsel), for appellant. I. The trial court's failure to provide meaningful notice to counsel of a substantive jury note is a mode of proceedings error that requires vacatur. ( People v O'Rama , 78 NY2d 270; People v Parker , 32 NY3d 49 ; People v Mack , 27 NY3d 534 ; People v DeRosario , 81 NY2d 801; People v Copeland , 175 AD3d 1316 .) II. Trial counsel rendered ineffective assistance by failing to adequately prepare for trial, resulting in multiple, prejudicial errors that denied Christopher Salas meaningful representation. ( Strickland v Washington , 466 US 668; People v Debellis , 40 NY3d 431 ; Padilla v Kentucky , 559 US 356; People v Oathout , 21 NY3d 127 ; People v Turner , 5 NY3d 476 .)
